articles.title: Beauty comes at a festive premium
articles.summary: New Delhi: Salons and services apps have doubled prices over last festive season amid sharp surge in demand for services such as dandiya luxe and garba glows to Durga deity looks and Navratri queens. Executives attributed the increase in prices to a combination of a surge in costs of key ingredients such as palm oil, and glass and plastic bottles and aerosols by 25-30% year-on-year on account of the West Asia war, pricing power and the withdrawal of input tax credit on salons last year.“As we speak, consumers are booking packages for new looks for each of the seven or nine days of Navratri and dandiya,” said CK Kumaravel, co-founder of Naturals Salons. “Prices have doubled over last year, since with the unexpected surge in demand, the industry is exercising high pricing power,” he said.Also Read: Festive cheer shifts beyond metros as consumer brands bet big on small-town IndiaOn Urban Company’s salon luxe, prices have touched Rs 5,000-plus, with services including make-up from global beauty brands such as Casmara and Mac.Since this is peak festive season with surge in demand specially from small towns, salons such as Madonna, Looks, Gitanjali and BBlunt have hiked prices to cash in on the season.“Further, the consequences of the withdrawal of input tax credit (ITC) late last year on salon chains, fitness centres, gyms and yoga clubs, despite reduction in GST slabs from 18% to 5%, are being passed on to the consumer,” said an executive at a beauty services platform. He requested not to be identified.“As salon operators and owners, we pay tax on equipment and raw materials. In the absence of refunds of input tax credit, our overall tax liability remains high and neutralises the reduction of GST on services,” he added.The West Asia war, which led to supply disruptions and spiked the prices of packaging materials, further hurt margins of the entire personal care sector. articles.title: Mutual funds close in on FPIs in Indian equity ownership
articles.summary: Mumbai: Indian mutual funds are closing in on foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) in their share of domestic equities, with the ownership gap narrowing to around 230 basis points, the lowest on record.The share of mutual funds' holdings in Indian equities rose to a record 11.7% in September, while that of FPIs fell below 14%, according to NSDL data. The FPI share has declined from a record 20% in May 2021, while the mutual fund share has climbed from around 7% during the same period. In January, the mutual fund share was 11%.The contraction in the ownership gap is an outcome of record selling by foreign investors along with unabated purchases by domestic mutual funds thanks to the deluge of retail flows into their equity products.134880107"In every market, normally local investors dominate and the same trend is emerging in India," said Samir Arora, founder and fund manager at Helios Capital Management. "It is reasonable to expect that in the medium term local institutional investors will own more of the market than foreign investors."Read more: Weekly Market Outlook: Nifty snaps 8-week losing streak, but can bulls reclaim the crucial 200-week moving average?FPIs' total equity assets under custody stood at ₹66.18 lakh crore in September, the lowest since March 2026, compared with a record ₹77.96 lakh crore in September 2024, when FPIs accounted for around 16.4% of Indian equities.Read more: ET Alpha Wealth Summit 2.0: What do Shah Rukh Khan and SIFs have in common? Radhika Gupta explainsMeanwhile, mutual funds' equity assets stood at around ₹55.14 lakh crore, up from around ₹20 lakh crore in April 2022. The corpus doubled to around ₹40 lakh crore by January 2024 and crossed ₹50 lakh crore in October 2025."Over time, mutual funds, high-net-worth individuals and family offices collectively are likely to account for a larger share of the market," said Ritesh Jain, founder of Canada-based Pinetree Macro.The changing ownership pattern is more pronounced among Nifty 500 companies, where domestic institutional investors (DIIs) have overtaken FPIs. DII holdings rose for the 9th consecutive quarter to a record 21% in Q1FY27, while FPI holdings fell to 17%, according to a Motilal Oswal Financial Services note.Sector Ownership DynamicsThe changing composition of the Indian economy could also be influencing FPI investment patterns. Foreign investors, which have historically had significant exposure to banks and IT companies, are now looking beyond these established sectors.The decline in FPI ownership has been visible across several key sectors, including IT, FMCG, consumer services, realty and financials. But, the trend has not been uniform, with foreign investors increasing their holdings in capital goods, metals and mining, telecom, services and healthcare.A recovery in corporate earnings will be key to a return of foreign investor appetite for Indian equities at a time when Asian markets such as Taiwan and Korea are hogging the limelight, boosted by AI-centric investments."If earnings grow at around 14-15% annually and the currency depreciates by around 2-3% a year, the resulting return for foreign investors would still be around 12%," said Arora.

articles.summary: Bangkok: The World Bank is in discussions with 30 to 40 countries about potential crisis aid to help them manage energy shocks and price increases triggered by the war in the Middle East, its president, Ajay Banga, told Reuters in an interview.Banga said the global economy had proven fairly resilient, in part due to big AI investments and adjustments in supply and demand for oil, which meant that few countries had sought the initial $25 billion in crisis funds that the World Bank had made available when the war began in late February.Also Read: World Bank raises India FY27 growth forecast to 7.1%, flags oil, El Niño risksHowever, a sharp spike in diesel and fertilizer prices and other factors, including the looming super El Nino weather effect, were adding to challenges facing developing countries, Banga said in an interview ahead of this week's annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank."There is pressure, and so I think maybe over the coming months, more countries will come for some slice of that first $50 to $60 billion," Banga said, referring to the initial $25 billion plus another $35 billion that countries could tap by diverting resources from already approved World Bank projects."We'll see, but we're ready. We're engaged. We're having conversations with a number of them, you know, 30 to 40 countries are in dialogue with us," he said.Many developing countries have been hit hard by the spike in energy prices and high interest rates that have increased borrowing costs at a time when their fiscal coffers are still depleted by measures taken during the COVID-19 pandemic and the spike in inflation following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.World Bank estimates show that developing countries owe external creditors about $400 billion in 2026, with interest payments alone comprising one-third of the total.Banga said more countries had shown interest in retooling existing projects than in tapping the immediate crisis window to address their liquidity needs. If the situation worsened, the Bank could make available as much as $100 billion in funds, he said, exceeding the $70 billion disbursed during the pandemic.The World Bank last month announced that it attracted a record $112 billion in private capital in the year ended June versus $69 billion a year earlier, and more than triple the 2022 total before Banga, a former Mastercard CEO, became president.Also Read: World Bank mobilises $112 billion in private capital for developing nationsThat was on top of the $123 billion invested from the bank's own resources for that year, for a combined $235 billion, Banga said, underscoring the importance of tapping all available resources, especially at a time when Western countries have sharply cut official bilateral development aid."There is no one answer that fits when the world has these kinds of issues. What you need to do is figure out how to cut your coat to suit your cloth," Banga said.Banga said he expected further gains in private capital flows in coming years, aided by expanded political risk guarantees from the bank's Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency, growth in local currency financing, and continued work on regulatory reforms that made it easier for foreign investors.The private capital jump was biggest in projects in upper-middle-income countries like Argentina or India, which accounted for $50 billion of the private capital, and lower-middle-income countries including Bangladesh and Angola, which accounted for $37 billion. But more work was needed to boost the roughly $3 billion in private capital flowing to low-income countries."In the smaller countries, it hasn't multiplied enough, and there are challenges," he said, noting the bank would announce some new initiatives this week aimed at ensuring micro-, small- and medium-sized businesses also had access to private capital.Banga said private capital growth was also regionally spread, with the largest increase seen in Latin America and the Caribbean, which accounted for $36.3 billion of last year's total, followed by Europe and Central Asia with $21.3 billion, South Asia with $19.2 billion and Africa with $22 billion.The top 10 recipient countries were Brazil, India, Turkey, Romania, Nigeria, Argentina, South Africa, Bangladesh, Mexico and Chile, the Bank said.Banga said the World Bank and IMF were working together to address the high debt levels plaguing many developing countries through a series of initiatives, including efforts to boost countries' domestic revenue collections.The Bank had already set up some debt-for-development swaps for Angola and Ivory Coast, and a portfolio-based guarantee for Argentina, and was working on over a dozen more projects."We've got 14 or 15 in the pipeline, helping them rotate out higher-priced old debt for newer-priced debt with our guarantees," with the difference then targeted at education, healthcare, water, or nature programs, he said.

articles.title: Republican lawmakers to bring Bill to block Trump's Russian diesel deal
articles.summary:
Republican Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick has declared that he would bring a bipartisan Bill to block President Donald Trump's move to lift sanctions on Russian diesel after talks with President Vladimir Putin.
Fitzpatrick's move has received support from outgoing Congressman Don Bacon, a Republican from Nebraska, who has decided to co-sponsor the legislation.
However, the move appears to be largely symbolic as the US House of Representatives will have a few months to pass as the term of the house expires in January.
"We will be introducing bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil," Fitzpatrick, the co-chair of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus, said in a post on x.
"It will be called the 'Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act'. It will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly," he said.
"I've already agreed to be an original cosponsor. Congress must make a stand," Bacon said in a post on X. Bacon is not seeking re-election

Mystery surrounds death of young worker in Russia studying deadly diseases
articles.summary:
The World Health Organisation (WHO) said Saturday it still doesn't know what caused the death of a young worker at a lab in Russia that focuses on plague and other illnesses.
The UN health agency has cited initial, unconfirmed reports suggesting pneumonic plague, a severe disease less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages. Pneumonic plague spreads from person to person, causing a severe form of pneumonia, but recovery rates are high if it is detected and treated in time.
WHO, in its first full Disease Outbreak News since the case emerged earlier this month, called for a continued investigation.
Russian health officials, it said, had conducted more than 5,500 tests and found no evidence of any dangerous pathogenic microorganisms.
"Additional clinical, epidemiological and laboratory information, including confirmation of the diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker, is required to improve confidence in the assessment," WHO said.
